items.body:
特斯拉自动驾驶团队出走创业：估值11亿美元，专门给机器人造虚拟世界

三名特斯拉自动驾驶仿真团队前负责人创办的 Zeromatter 正式亮相，估值达到 11 亿美元，累计融资 1.6 亿美元。公司已有超过 130 名员工，其中约 40 人也来自特斯拉。

三名创始人此前都是游戏开发者。CEO Ian Glow 曾参与开发 Minecraft，后来带领特斯拉的仿真团队，为自动驾驶和 Optimus 人形机器人搭建虚拟测试环境。

Zeromatter 把这套技术做成了独立产品。客户可以在虚拟世界里训练自动驾驶汽车、无人机和机器人，反复测试危险或罕见场景。比如模拟儿童突然从停放的汽车后方冲出，或者让机器人尝试抓取、安装零件，不必在现实中冒险。

它的重点是让模拟结果尽可能接近现实。公司自研了物理引擎和传感器模拟系统，不仅要还原画面，还要模拟碰撞、摩擦、摄像头误差等细节。团队会购买真实设备，在实验室测量各种情况，再与虚拟结果逐一比较。

Glow 认为，机器人走路、跑步已经取得很大进展，真正困难的是让双手准确操作物体。Zeromatter 正在重点攻克这类需要精确模拟接触和摩擦的任务。

特朗普拟选20多家AI「国家冠军」：英伟达、OpenAI、Anthropic都在名单上

特朗普政府准备把英伟达、亚马逊、微软、OpenAI、Anthropic 等 20 多家公司列为美国 AI「国家冠军」，帮助它们到海外抢生意，与中国科技企业竞争。

入选后能得到什么好处？美国政府会帮这些公司向外国政府推销产品、协调海外项目，还能优先审查芯片等技术的出口许可证，并协助申请联邦融资。

美国还打算把芯片、数据中心、AI 模型和应用软件打包出售。比如外国政府要建设 AI 数据中心，可以直接采购一整套美国技术，不必分别寻找芯片厂商、云服务商和模型公司。

这项计划早在 2025 年 7 月就已启动。今年 7 月，美国商务部称收到 78 份申请，涉及从芯片到 AI 应用的整套出口方案。这次准备公布的是重点扶持名单，预计由商务部长 Howard Lutnick 在未来一周宣布。

英伟达的处境尤其微妙。黄仁勋刚因丑闻辞去 CEO 职务，公司对华芯片销售也正受到更严格的审查，但特朗普政府仍打算把英伟达列入名单。与此同时，商务部还准备收紧规定，防止高端芯片通过其他渠道流入中国。

items.body:
谷歌Antigravity密集上新：电脑操作即将上线，Carbon提速、手机App也在做

谷歌 Antigravity 负责人 Varun Mohan 宣布，Antigravity 已将 Gemini 4 Argon、Carbon、Hydrogen 三款模型的上下文窗口扩大一倍。每轮对话触发的上下文压缩次数可减少约 3.5 倍，让 Agent 在长任务中少花时间整理历史信息。

Varun 还透露，Antigravity 即将加入原生电脑操作（Computer Use）功能，让 Agent 能够直接操作桌面软件。

不少开发者在 Varun 和 Google DeepMind 的 Gemini 后训练负责人 Melvin Johnson 的评论区抱怨，Carbon 虽然能力很强，但运行速度太慢。Melvin 承认正在提速，并透露团队已有兼顾速度与模型能力的方案。Varun 则表示，此次上下文扩容也能减少压缩耗时，加快任务完成。

有用户希望推出每月 300 美元、500 美元的更高额度套餐，Varun 回复称「正在做」。Melvin 还透露，Antigravity 移动 App 已在规划当中。

过去一周，Antigravity 还接连上线 Gemini 4 Carbon、Hydrogen 两款模型，推出 Swarm 多 Agent 并行协作、Orchestrator 不同模型分工，以及用 Python 编排 Agent 任务的 Dynamic Workflows。

items.title: How Revolut raises ambition without lowering the bar
items.summary: Discover how Revolut uses OpenAI models and Codex to cut coding time by 30–60%, scale financial crime investigations, and innovate without compromising security.
items.body:
November 16, 2026

With OpenAI models and Codex, Revolut is giving its teams more room to solve complex problems—from software engineering to financial crime.

Contact sales

Company size: Enterprise

Region: Global

Industry: Technology, Finance

Products: ChatGPT, API, Codex

30–60%

Reduction in coding time from task start to feature merge

One day

To turn seven years of design documentation into AI-readable context

1–2 days

Saved on security code review with Codex

Revolut⁠(opens in a new window) was built to challenge the way people interact with money. That ambition now stretches across more than 40 markets, 800,000 businesses and a consumer base that’s grown by 23% in the last 12 months.

Add to that a company culture that expects small, lean teams to move quickly and it’s no surprise that ChatGPT and Codex have proven a natural fit.

“The perfect description for a high-caliber Revolut person is someone who can identify a problem really quickly, deduce the solution, design four scenarios, identify the best one of those four then take it to market,” says Kim Maniovich, Revolut’s Global Head of Business Marketing.

“Partnering with OpenAI enables us to build a lot of these solutions in a way that’s incredibly lean, cost-efficient and really tailored to the unique way that we work.”

But moving faster is only part of the opportunity. For Revolut, the bigger question is what becomes possible when talented people spend less time on the mechanics of getting things done—and more time tackling problems that could fundamentally change financial services.

As Revolut grows, so does the complexity of protecting its customers. According to one report⁠(opens in a new window), over half of adults worldwide reported a scam encounter in 2025.

For Revolut, every transaction creates another opportunity to identify suspicious activity, investigate potential risks and implement robust and tailored protections for its customers. But the sheer volume of those transactions far outstrips the human resources available to any bank.

“The biggest problem we can tackle with AI today is the scaling of humans versus the demand that we get,” says AI Lead David Abitbol. That’s why one of Revolut’s largest AI applications is a FinCrime agent powered by OpenAI models.

Rather than requiring investigators to work through every eligible case manually, the agent can examine information, apply Revolut’s rules and complete the defined process automatically.

The release of GPT‑5.5 was a turning point. It was then, says Abitbol, that the models had become capable and cost-effective enough for Revolut to delegate screening and investigation workflows entirely to the agent. The result is greater capacity to monitor transactions without increasing investigator headcount at the same rate as demand.

That, adds Information Security Engineer Mo Amiri, “translates directly into stronger protection and a more resilient system our customers can trust.”

‘Move fast but build trust’ could easily be Revolut’s internal engineering slogan. While Abitbol points out that Codex has delivered a 30-60% reduction in coding time, he’s also clear that certain guardrails are non-negotiable.

“We have a systematic framework where anyone in the company who’s building anything with AI has the same set of standards across development, A/B testing, and business metric prediction,” he says. “So every engineer is held to the same standard of quality across the company. We started to get enough intelligence for reasonable costs where we could increasingly delegate initial investigations and screenings to the agent.”

For Senior Platform Engineer Dmitry Pitik, that 30-60% reduction in coding time became tangible while he was building an internal code-review service. He designed the system, broke it into features and initially assumed he’d need a development team to implement it.

“I realised I don’t need a whole team of developers to implement this,” he recalls. “I can just launch different agents and assign each of them a particular task.” Codex became his implementation team, while Dmitry spent more time designing the system, planning the work and reviewing what came back.

This is a pattern that Abitbol has seen across Revolut. As Codex returns capacity to engineers they’re using that reclaimed time “to spend more time discussing design and the best solution. So we spend more time designing instead of implementing.”

That doesn’t remove the need for engineering expertise, it just changes where that expertise is applied. “Every developer is responsible for the code they produce, and we don’t blindly trust AI,” Pitik says. The result is a different division of work: AI can help with implementation, while engineers devote more attention to the decisions that determine whether the software is useful, reliable and worth building.

That overhead is worth it. As Codex works on one task, Pitik can work in parallel on another. That kind of multitasking is essential in a company where, as Kim Maniovich explains, the average employee has “three different jobs.” Using Codex creates a virtuous (if challenging) flywheel where “month on month the targets we’re setting get more aggressive, but also more attainable. And so the bar keeps moving up. AI is making that possible.”

Examples of what Revolut has been able to do with this new-found capacity include developing a tool to build web UIs for internal apps and external-facing products.

Or turning seven years of design documentation into AI-readable context in a single day, creating a foundation for tools intended to help designers work more effectively. The exercise illustrates how AI can make accumulated organisational knowledge more accessible, reducing the effort required to work with complex systems. “We can shift focus from the things which are important but hard to do without AI to the things which matter for customers,” says Senior Designer Dmytro Pavlov.

“I realised I don’t need a whole team of developers. I can just launch different agents and assign them a task.”

—Dmitry Pitik, Senior Platform Engineer, Revolut

Mo Amiri’s job is to make sure all of this speed is matched by security—not just for customers but for Revolut’s own employees. That gives him two views of AI at once: how it can help Revolut investigate a problem, and what teams need before they can deploy it safely.

In a phishing investigation, for example, an analyst once had to gather an email, inspect its links and attachments, trace the sender and assemble the evidence manually. “With stronger AI tools, we can uncover those connections instantly, and dig deeper into the questions that really matter,” he says.

While AI does the legwork and presents an investigator with a structured case, it’s still down to the individual to review the original records, decide whether the explanation makes sense and approve any action.

Amiri applies the same thinking when teams bring new AI applications into Revolut. He follows the complete chain: what information the system sees, where that information goes, which tools it can reach, what it can do with that access and what happens when something fails. He also tests whether apparently convincing conclusions are actually supported by the evidence.

“The most critical decision is always about accountability,” he says. “If an AI tool suggests a code change, a human engineer needs to understand that change well enough to stand by it. That directly drives how we design the review process, giving developers the context they need without cluttering their everyday workflow.”

For Revolut, safeguards aren’t separate from innovation. They help establish the conditions under which teams can confidently adopt more capable technology. “That’s how you earn real confidence in AI,” he explains, “by making thoughtful decisions upfront and testing as you go.”

“You earn real confidence in AI by making thoughtful decisions upfront and testing as you go.”

—Mo Amiri, Information Security Engineer, Revolut

• 30–60% reduction in coding time from task start to feature merge

• One engineer built an internal code-review service by delegating implementation tasks to multiple Codex agents

• One day to transform existing design-system documentation developed over roughly seven years into AI-readable context

• One to two days saved on one substantial security code-review task

• More transactions screened through the FinCrime agent without scaling investigators one for one

• Start with a problem worth solving. Revolut has put AI to work where demand is growing fastest and the stakes for customers are highest.

• Use speed to raise ambition, not lower standards. Time saved on coding and investigation creates room for better design, harder questions and more consequential work.

• Keep people on the hook. AI can gather evidence, write code and recommend action. A person still needs to understand the work well enough to stand behind it.

• Build trust before you scale. Be clear about what a system can see, what it can do and what happens when it fails—then test those decisions as you go.

• Make your knowledge usable. AI works better when it can reach clear, well-organised context. The same exercise often shows where the organisation itself needs to be clearer.

Revolut has already shown how AI can increase the amount and complexity of work its teams can attempt. Its next opportunity is to carry that combination of capability, judgment and design into the way customers interact with their money.

But moving faster is only part of the opportunity. For Revolut, the bigger question is what becomes possible when talented people spend less time on the mechanics of getting things done—and more time tackling problems that could fundamentally change financial services.
As Revolut grows, so does the complexity of protecting its customers. According to one report⁠(opens in a new window), over half of adults worldwide reported a scam encounter in 2025.

For Revolut, every transaction creates another opportunity to identify suspicious activity, investigate potential risks and implement robust and tailored protections for its customers. But the sheer volume of those transactions far outstrips the human resources available to any bank.

“The biggest problem we can tackle with AI today is the scaling of humans versus the demand that we get,” says AI Lead David Abitbol. That’s why one of Revolut’s largest AI applications is a FinCrime agent powered by OpenAI models.
Rather than requiring investigators to work through every eligible case manually, the agent can examine information, apply Revolut’s rules and complete the defined process automatically.

It was then, says Abitbol, that the models had become capable and cost-effective enough for Revolut to delegate screening and investigation workflows entirely to the agent. The result is greater capacity to monitor transactions without increasing investigator headcount at the same rate as demand.
That, adds Information Security Engineer Mo Amiri, “translates directly into stronger protection and a more resilient system our customers can trust.”

‘Move fast but build trust’ could easily be Revolut’s internal engineering slogan. While Abitbol points out that Codex has delivered a 30-60% reduction in coding time, he’s also clear that certain guardrails are non-negotiable.

“We have a systematic framework where anyone in the company who’s building anything with AI has the same set of standards across development, A/B testing, and business metric prediction,” he says. “So every engineer is held to the same standard of quality across the company. “I realised I don’t need a whole team of developers to implement this,” he recalls. “I can just launch different agents and assign each of them a particular task.” Codex became his implementation team, while Dmitry spent more time designing the system, planning the work and reviewing what came back.

This is a pattern that Abitbol has seen across Revolut. As Codex returns capacity to engineers they’re using that reclaimed time “to spend more time discussing design and the best solution. So we spend more time designing instead of implementing.”

That doesn’t remove the need for engineering expertise, it just changes where that expertise is applied. “Every developer is responsible for the code they produce, and we don’t blindly trust AI,” Pitik says. The result is a different division of work: AI can help with implementation, while engineers devote more attention to the decisions that determine whether the software is useful, reliable and worth building.

That overhead is worth it. As Codex works on one task, Pitik can work in parallel on another. That kind of multitasking is essential in a company where, as Kim Maniovich explains, the average employee has “three different jobs.” Using Codex creates a virtuous (if challenging) flywheel where “month on month the targets we’re setting get more aggressive, but also more attainable. And so the bar keeps moving up. AI is making that possible.”

乌兰察布AI基建有多疯狂：25GW算力项目已签约，近3万人同时赶工

前段时间，美国研究机构 SemiAnalysis 专程来到内蒙古乌兰察布，将规划 800MW 的远景星河基地称为「中国版 Stargate」。然而，这座足以与美国超大型 AI 数据中心相提并论的园区，在乌兰察布只能算冰山一角。一场规模更加庞大的算力建设，正在这片草原上铺开。

根据当地公开数据，截至今年 10 月中旬，乌兰察布累计签约 109 个算力中心项目，签约 IT 供电容量超过 25GW，规划机架规模超过 700 万架。

《晚点》记者近期在乌兰察布实地走访了 72 小时。当地察哈尔高新区就有 22 个算力项目同时施工，近 3 万名工人在不同工地赶工。

在巴音片区，十几辆几十米长的板车排成一排，运载着数百个尚未拆封的服务器机柜。道路两侧有 4 个数据中心同时建设，到了晚上，塔吊和挖掘机还在施工。一些工地每三个月就要完成一栋机房楼。

客户要求的交付时间也越来越短。远景 AI 智算中心 CTO 胡兴赞透露，过去客户能接受 12 个月的建设周期，后来缩短到 9 个月、6 个月，现在甚至要求两三个月交付。

因为 GPU 太贵，机房延期一天，就可能让价值数十亿元的计算设备继续闲置。一名项目负责人透露，如果未能按合同交付机房，每晚一天就要赔偿客户 50 万元，一个月就是 1500 万元。

为了赶工，建设方开始提前拿地、建设厂房、采购大型设备。部分配电系统直接在工厂组装成模块，运到现场后再连接。原本需要 10 天的安装工作，可以压缩到 2 天。

OpenAI为何迟迟不发新旗舰模型？内部员工爆料：公司已经留下太多「伤疤」

OpenAI 上一次更新 Astra 旗舰模型还是 9 月初，原定 10 月推出的后续版本也被取消。近日，OpenAI 安全团队员工 Joe 在一条已经删除的帖子中透露，公司内部的研发文化已经彻底转向「安全优先」，甚至可以说 OpenAI 已经变成了一家「安全公司」。

Joe 表示，如今安全问题贯穿公司内部的日常讨论，就连顶尖 AI 研究员，也要花大量时间与安全团队合作，研究如何安全地进行强化学习训练。他自己几个月前一度想辞职，如今看到公司的变化，决定留下。

这场转变源于今年 7 月的一次严重事故。当时，OpenAI 的内部模型在安全测试中突破隔离环境，擅自连接互联网，甚至入侵了 Hugging Face 的系统。9 月又有内部模型利用网络配置漏洞，绕过限制访问外网。

OpenAI 随后多次暂停前沿模型训练，抽调工程师加固系统。公司约四分之一的产品工程师被调去处理安全问题。一次内部安全攻坚就动员了 250 多人，覆盖 100 多个服务领域。

研发流程也被重新设计。OpenAI 花费数千亿 Token，让 AI 反复攻击自家的训练环境，寻找漏洞。公司还建立了 Control Room，持续监控模型运行，发现危险行为后，最多 35 秒就能阻止模型继续输出。

这些安全要求已经直接影响模型发布。9 月底，OpenAI 取消了原定 10 月推出的新一代 Astra 旗舰模型。安全负责人 Saachi Jain 解释称，新模型虽然执行任务更加积极，但在遵守用户授权范围、清楚汇报自身操作等方面反而不如上一代。安全团队因此建议取消发布，研究管理层最终接受了这一决定。

OpenAI 已于 10 月 1 日恢复此前暂停的前沿强化学习训练，但新一代 Astra 旗舰至今仍未公布发布日期。Joe 认为，管理层如今也认识到，只有先确保足够的安全性，才能继续推进更强模型的研发。他表示，过去的教训给公司留下了不少伤疤。

items.title: Our first phase of embedded assessments
items.summary: OpenAI begins embedded assessments with Apollo Research, METR, and Transluce, and Goodfire to independently evaluate model alignment, safeguards, and monitoring systems.
items.body:
November 16, 2026

Safety

We have signed agreements with four independent assessors—Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire—for our first phase of embedded assessments. As AI capabilities advance rapidly and the potential risks grow, public reporting from independent assessments can give people a clearer view of how labs are evaluating and managing those risks.

Embedded assessments give independent experts deep access to a lab’s internal models and systems to assess model alignment and the effectiveness of safeguards over an extended period of time, especially where relevant to our safety cases. Based on what each evaluation needs, assessors receive access to some of the same internal resources our researchers use, including model checkpoints, source code, training and evaluation data, monitoring systems, technical documentation, and discussions with the researchers and engineers responsible for the work. This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated.

Our initial assessments focus on alignment and safeguards for models during training and internal use, complementing our safety cases. They build on our priorities and principles for third party assessments and years of work with third party evaluators, including a recent pilot assessment of our internal monitoring systems⁠(opens in a new window) with deep internal access and an investigation of the Hugging Face incident⁠(opens in a new window). We’ll use what we learn to deepen our work with independent experts in the coming months. These efforts also support our commitments under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, where we agreed to independent assessments of our safety controls. These collaborations can contribute to stronger shared standards for independent assessment and public transparency across the industry.

In this pilot assessment, Apollo Research⁠(opens in a new window) will assess whether models could covertly work against their developers’ intentions and whether our safeguards would detect such behavior. Drawing on evidence from training, safety testing, and internal use. Apollo will assess four claims in two stages:

1. Training did not incentivize subversion.

2. Strong evaluations and red teaming do not elicit subversion.

3. Models have not attempted subversion during internal use.

4. Reasoning behind subversion would be detectable.

For the first stage of Apollo’s assessment, we’ll provide access to selected public and unreleased models and training checkpoints, relevant training data and evaluation results, training intervention records, monitoring systems and flagged behaviors, and researchers who can provide context, alongside the tools and compute needed to conduct independent testing.

Goodfire⁠(opens in a new window) will embed interpretability researchers and use the Goodfire platform to analyze model internals. The main objective of their assessment is training run monitoring, debugging, and alignment. The primary audience for their assessments are internal OpenAI researchers, who will use their findings to make safety improvements. Goodfire will also publish learnings and findings as the collaboration progresses.

We intend to conduct two assessments with METR⁠(opens in a new window), focused on model alignment and monitoring:

• Alignment assessment: For the first phase, METR will assess misaligned behavior in our largest reinforcement learning run to date, including failures that our existing tests and monitors may have missed. Within the selected run and agreed access, resources, and safety arrangements, METR would independently set assessment priorities and iterate on searches, analyses, and elicitation experiments. Access will include sampling relevant checkpoints, training and eval rollouts, and misalignment monitoring records for this run. For this first phase, the assessment will focus on our largest frontier RL run.

• Monitor assessment: We recently worked with METR to conduct a monitor stress testing exercise. We have preliminarily agreed to conduct another monitor assessment⁠(opens in a new window) which we intend to be broader, but this is pending mutual agreement on the assessment scope.

Transluce⁠(opens in a new window) will conduct an initial assessment of our post-training alignment evaluations, examining their quality and coverage. For the initial assessment, we will provide Transluce with access to selected public and unreleased models, our post-training alignment evaluations and relevant results, supporting model behavior data and safety case documentation, and researchers who can provide context, alongside the tools and compute needed to conduct independent testing.

OpenAI and Transluce also share the intent to conduct a follow-on assessment of approximately eight weeks in early 2027, with broader access to additional models, deeper access to our alignment evaluations, and information on how evaluation results inform model release decisions.

We’ve developed protocols and processes with input from the assessors to balance deep access with security, confidentiality, oversight, and the independence and integrity of assessments. We are sharing them to shed light on how we will work with embedded assessors, and to advance discussion about norms for embedded assessments, which have yet to be standardized. We expect that these will need to evolve as we learn more about how to best conduct these assessments. Especially in the early stages of embedded assessments, we expect technical access challenges, space constraints, evolving security protocols, and other unexpected issues to arise. We hope to work through these challenges collaboratively with our embedded assessors and share lessons learned.

Each engagement begins with an agreed scope and the access, resources, and safety arrangements needed to conduct a rigorous assessment. Some assessments test specific safety claims; others give assessors room to discover unexpected failure modes within a defined system or training run. In both cases, assessors need the freedom to follow evidence, refine their methods, and propose further assessments when findings warrant it. We also have a process for addressing additional access needs as assessments develop. When direct access could expose our most sensitive IP, such as model weights or architecture, we will consider alternatives, including pairing assessors with OpenAI researchers to run analyses.

Assessors who need access to sensitive confidential information will work on site at OpenAI offices and be provided OpenAI devices to conduct their work. The primary purpose is to protect the security of the information they access. Working onsite also gives assessors the opportunity to engage with dedicated staff who can help them navigate their access and provide context for their assessments. We also expect our embedded assessors to follow at minimum the same security standards as OpenAI employees when running experiments and evaluations.

Our Safety and Security Committee (SSC), an independent oversight committee of the OpenAI Foundation’s Board, will have visibility into the embedded assessment and the ability to exercise their oversight responsibilities before, during, and at their conclusion. They will receive unredacted reports, and both the assessors and the SSC will be able to speak with each other during the assessment, including privately. Disagreements among OpenAI and any evaluator will be escalated to the Safety Advisory Group and OpenAI executives, who will have a specified time period to resolve them, and the SSC will be notified of any such disagreements promptly when escalated. If a disagreement remains, the matter will be referred to the SSC for resolution.

Discussions with employees help assessors understand internal information and the context behind the work. OpenAI will authorize and provide guidance to staff members who can speak to assessors, and assessors may request additional staff to speak with as needed. To encourage open, candid conversations and protect the privacy of our staff, these discussions are off the record, meaning that they can inform the assessments but cannot be published or attributed to employees. Through a separate attestation pathway, assessors can request OpenAI-attested statements verifying, correcting, or clarifying something they learned in conversation with employees. These statements are not attributed to individuals or intended to characterize individual views. Assessors may publish statements that OpenAI attests to, or disclose that OpenAI declined to attest to a statement.

Managing conflicts of interest clearly and transparently—including those involving personal relationships, financial interests, and other issues—is important to the integrity and independence of evaluations. Cool-off periods also need to be designed carefully, so assessors can work responsibly across labs while handling competitive information sensitively. We are working with our assessors to develop clear processes for both conflicts and cool-off periods, including allowing for flexibility in mitigations and transparency in decisions to request recusal.

Assessors maintain independence in publishing their assessments, but we will retain the right to redact confidential information, consistent with our previous third-party engagements. We may also request responsible disclosure delays to allow time to act on findings that could pose security or safety risks and remediate issues that remain.

Public reporting will help people understand the findings and their limitations, while more detailed confidential reports give oversight bodies the evidence they need to act. We want these assessments to improve how we identify and address risks, and give the public a clearer basis for judging our safety work.

These assessments bring an independent perspective to our ongoing alignment and safety work. Public reporting on their findings will make that work more transparent and provide greater assurance about how risks are being identified and addressed. We expect this first phase of assessments to lead to longer-term, consistent embedded engagements over time that can continuously provide third party safety signals and recommended improvements on our most load bearing safety claims and safety cases.

We’ll continue working with multiple independent third parties to help build a healthy assessment ecosystem with diverse expertise and approaches. Some investigations need sustained, on-site work with sensitive systems; others primarily evaluate deployed or soon to be deployed models or review public documentation.

In the coming months, we’ll support external assessments across a broader range of safety questions. We are also exploring future embedded assessments that would examine compliance with our safety frameworks, as well as our organizational culture and processes. We are committed to expanding this work and helping build the capacity and shared standards needed to sustain it.

items.body:
Qwen4-Max追近Kimi：综合差3分、成本低11%，但编程差距仍明显

独立评测机构 Artificial Analysis 公布 Qwen4-Max 正式版成绩。在最高 xhigh 推理档位下，模型综合智能指数达到 43 分，比上一代 Qwen3.8-Max 的 34 分提高 9 分，距离 Kimi K3.1 Pro 的 46 分还差 3 分。

Qwen4-Max 在全部 9 项评测中均超过前代。高难知识推理测试 HLE-Diamond 的正确率从 24% 提升至 45%，企业软件自动化测试提高 17 个百分点。在模拟真实业务文件处理的 AA-Briefcase 中，Qwen4-Max 获得 1686 Elo，略高于 Kimi K3.1 Pro 的 1674。

编程能力仍是短板。Terminal-Bench 4.0 测试中，Qwen4-Max 得分 48%，明显落后 Kimi K3.1 Pro 的 67%。在考查真实开源项目开发能力的 FrontierCode 2.0 中，两者均为 26%，落后腾讯 Hy4 的 31%。

成本方面，Qwen4-Max 的平均单任务费用为 3.27 美元，上一代为 10.02 美元，降低约 67%，也比 Kimi K3.1 Pro 的 3.68 美元便宜约 11%。

除了 API 降价，模型本身也减少了 Token 消耗。Qwen4-Max 每项任务平均输出约 10.5 万 Token，比上一代的 17.1 万减少 39%。不过，Kimi K3.1 Pro 只需要约 7.2 万 Token。

Codex「模型已满」报错大幅减少：受影响用户占比从6.82%降至0.085%

OpenAI 核心产品负责人 Tibo Sottiaux 晒出一张内部统计图，表示团队可能终于解决了长期困扰用户的「模型容量已满」报错。

数据显示，10 月 19 日，约 6.82% 的 Codex 日活跃用户至少遇到一次以容量错误结束的请求。到 11 月 12 日，这一比例已降至 0.085%。

此前，大量用户反映，即使订阅额度充足，Codex 仍会突然提示模型已满，要求切换模型。正在执行的编程任务会直接中断，换模型也未必有用。

这次修复主要围绕自动重试机制展开。10 月 15 日至 11 月 6 日，OpenAI 先后进行了 6 轮调整。服务器过载时，会告诉 Codex 应该等待多久再试。客户端收到指令后，可以等待并自动重试，尽量避免任务直接终止。OpenAI 在此之前还增加了推理算力。

有人调侃，Codex 报错减少可能是因为用户都跑去使用 Claude Opus 5.5 了。

腾讯首次推出Flash档模型：224B总参数、12B激活，部分办公任务成本降超20倍

腾讯混元正式发布首款以 Flash 命名的模型 Hy4 flash，在 Hy4 系列中形成旗舰与低成本 Flash 两个档位。

Hy4 flash 的总参数为 224B，其中 64B 是 Engram 记忆参数，每次推理激活 12B。相比 Hy4 的 770B 总参数、49B 激活参数，规模明显缩小，但依然支持多模态和 100 万 Token 上下文。

Engram 是 DeepSeek 此前提出的条件记忆技术。它把部分常见文本模式存进可快速查询的记忆表，让模型通过查表获取信息，减少重复计算。

Hy4 flash 每百万 Token 输入仅 0.5 元、输出 2 元、缓存命中 0.02 元。相比 Hy4 的 API 刊例价，分别降低 12 倍、9 倍和 15 倍。不过，Hy4 目前另有五折限时优惠，实际价差会小于刊例价差。

腾讯官方测试中，PPT 协同编辑得分从 Hy4 的 78.9 降至 74.0，但单次任务成本从 1.714 元降至 0.105 元，约为原来的十六分之一。自动化任务得分也仅从 56.2 降至 52.2，每任务成本则从 0.908 元降至 0.038 元。

复杂任务的差距更大。在 Terminal-Bench 4.0 终端操作测试中，Hy4 flash 仅得 19.2 分，旗舰 Hy4 为 44.4 分。ProgramBench 编程测试也从 30.0 分降至 16.0 分。

items.body:
November 16, 2026

Product

Introducing computer-use agents, a new healthcare model configuration, and new healthcare plugins that work across healthcare software to get real work done.

Contact our sales team

Healthcare teams need to piece together information from the EHR, hospital policies, scheduling systems, and payer portals to deliver care and manage operations. With ChatGPT for Healthcare, we’re bringing the tools teams already use and the medical evidence they need into one platform to help them spend less time navigating systems and more time caring for patients.

Today, we’re sharing advances in computer use that help AI agents carry out multi-step work across existing healthcare software. We’re also improving how trusted clinical search finds, evaluates, and cites medical evidence. A new healthcare model configuration in the Responses API lets developers build trusted clinical search into their own applications. And we’re expanding our healthcare plugin ecosystem with more than 20 new plugins.

Together, these capabilities help healthcare teams find the information they need, make decisions grounded in medical evidence, and carry out next steps across the systems they already use.

Organizations often need to move information between disconnected systems to prepare documentation, coordinate care, and complete administrative tasks. Computer-use agents can help with these steps by navigating the software that teams already use: reading screens, clicking, typing, and moving between applications.

Today, we’re sharing advances in computer-use agents for healthcare, including more capable, safe, and affordable models for clinical and administrative workflows, and access controls and audit logs for secure deployments. We’re also sharing our work with healthcare organizations that are deploying agents, including Abridge, Ambience, Cigna Healthcare, and CVS Health, to process referrals, move documents between systems, and bring together the information care teams need. In the demo below, a clinician uses Voice in the ChatGPT app to ask for help following up on an MRI request. The agent reviews the chart and drafts an order and patient reply for review.

Healthcare organizations can start with a workflow that spans existing applications, set which applications agents can access, and establish clear controls for which steps require human review. To support HIPAA-compliant workflows involving protected health information, organizations must use eligible services covered by their BAA with OpenAI, apply required security and retention settings, and extend protections to connected systems. Content shared with ChatGPT for Healthcare is not used to train models.

Read more about our computer use research, customer stories, and demonstrations in Advancing computer-use agents for healthcare teams⁠.

We’re improving trusted clinical search in ChatGPT for Healthcare and ChatGPT for Clinicians, including how ChatGPT finds, evaluates, and cites medical evidence. These updates help clinicians connect relevant evidence to clinical questions and translate it into practical next steps, with citations they can inspect.

To measure the impact of these updates, in a blind evaluation, physicians reviewed responses to real-world clinical questions across multiple specialties, including multi-turn conversations. In over 1300 reviews, physicians rated the updated experience more highly across all eight dimensions evaluated, including factual correctness, safety, actionability, and source authoritativeness.

Developers can now bring cited medical evidence into their applications with a healthcare configuration of select OpenAI models, including GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. Available through the Responses API today, the configuration pairs the models with a harness tailored to clinical questions and trusted clinical search.

GPT‑6.2 Astra with the healthcare configuration ranked first among the systems we evaluated on HealthBench Professional, a benchmark of 525 challenging tasks written by physicians to test how well AI can answer questions about patient care, draft clinical documentation, and synthesize medical evidence. It earned a length-adjusted score of 74.4%, 6.3 percentage points ahead of the highest-scoring non-OpenAI system, Claude Fable 5.2 with web search.

During a visit, clinicians rely on rapid point-of-care responses. On HealthBench Professional, GPT‑6.2 Astra configured for healthcare delivered higher-quality responses in an average of 23 seconds, compared with nearly three minutes for the same model using general-purpose web search even when using its highest reasoning setting.

For developers deploying these tools at scale, cost per response matters too. In a separate comparison on the same benchmark, Astra with the healthcare configuration scored higher than Claude Fable 5.2 with web search at less than half the API cost per scored response ($1.37 vs. $2.90), with both systems at their highest reasoning settings.

Customers are already seeing the value of building with the new model configuration.

items.title: Advancing computer-use agents for healthcare teams
items.body:
November 16, 2026

Product

Healthcare is fragmented, and teams often need to move information between systems manually before a patient can get care. When a clinician recommends an MRI, for example, the information an insurer needs may be in a patient’s medical record, but a team member still needs to retrieve it and enter it into a separate portal to complete an authorization request.

Computer-use agents carry out multi-step workflows by clicking, typing, and moving between applications. In healthcare, this enables AI to help with repetitive workflows in the software teams already use.

Today, we’re sharing new results measuring model performance, safety, and cost in clinical and administrative workflows. We’re also sharing the ways we’re working with leading healthcare organizations like Abridge, Ambience, Cigna Healthcare, and CVS Health to advance and apply computer use, across authorization requests, referrals, discharge planning, and outreach between visits.

Healthcare teams, developers, and individual clinicians can access these capabilities today through the OpenAI API, ChatGPT for Healthcare, and ChatGPT for Clinicians. Organizations can support HIPAA-compliant workflows, configure approvals and agent access, and record audit logs for secure deployments.

To show how a computer-use agent can help a clinician and an authorization specialist work on the same MRI request, we built a demo using synthetic patient data. A patient messages their clinician about lower back pain. A computer-use agent reviews the patient’s visit notes, physical therapy records, and prior imaging in the EHR. It drafts an MRI order, an encounter note, and a reply to the patient for the clinician to review. The agent then uses the same records to prepare a prior authorization request in the insurer’s portal for an authorization specialist to review.

We evaluated GPT‑6 Astra on tasks clinicians handle in their EHR inboxes. These tasks, shaped by physician input, require Astra to carry out multi-step workflows designed to test both clinical reasoning over longitudinal patient context and navigation of complex interfaces. Reviewers examined the model’s actions alongside the notes, orders, and patient messages it produced, assessing whether the work would be helpful and clinically safe in the context of the task.

Clinical safety was assessed by evaluating whether inaccuracies, omissions, or actions in the model’s work could plausibly lead to patient harm. Overall, 99% of 325 reviewed tasks were rated safe. Physicians rated helpfulness on a five-point scale, selecting “very helpful” or “extremely helpful” in 93% of 646 assessments.

We also evaluated computer-use agents for administrative tasks, such as prior authorizations, appeals, and medical equipment orders. On HealthAdminBench⁠(opens in a new window), an independent benchmark from Stanford researchers measuring performance on common administrative workflows, GPT‑6 Astra earned 94.3% of available rubric points, while GPT‑6 Luna earned 91.8%, despite costing 98% less at 8.5 cents per task. Both models were evaluated at maximum reasoning effort. These results show progress toward capable, affordable agents for high-volume administrative workflows.

Our partners build software used in hundreds of health systems, coordinate care for members globally, and deliver care to hundreds of millions of patients. The following examples showcase how organizations are developing, piloting, and deploying computer-use applications to save time, solve critical problems, and improve patient care.

CVS Health is using OpenAI’s computer-use capabilities to automate repetitive work across clinical systems, including sending documents, processing referrals, and supporting specialist consults. The agents navigate existing applications to complete steps that APIs do not fully support.

In one production workflow, an agent cleared a months-long document-sending backlog over a weekend. Another handles the system steps for tens of thousands of consults each day, helping team members focus on work that needs their expertise. CVS Health uses validation checks and human oversight, with screenshots and action records to verify actions and application state. CVS Health is open sourcing its Agent Kit⁠(opens in a new window), built with OpenAI’s Agents SDK, which packages this approach as a repeatable process for broader use.

“Less time on administrative work means more time for care. That’s a win for our teams and everyone we serve.”

—Lagan Khare, Executive Director, Engineering, CVS Health.

Data remains within the CVS Health enterprise-controlled infrastructure, governed by their enterprise AI Governance team and established responsible AI policies. Production data is not used to train foundation models.

Abridge is developing computer-use agents to help clinicians carry out care plans across use cases and applications they use daily, including those without APIs. Their planned inpatient use case builds on the clinical conversation, adding EHR information and nurse and clinician context to identify what needs attention and to coordinate next steps.

For example, a clinician can ask the Abridge Assistant to help resolve a patient’s discharge barriers. Agents can work concurrently on medication access and home-health coordination, using computer interaction alongside calls and messages. The clinician stays focused on the patient and is brought in for decisions requiring clinical judgment.

As part of The Cigna Group’s broader collaboration with OpenAI, Cigna Healthcare is using OpenAI’s frontier models alongside its own clinical expertise to bring together relevant information across systems and give care teams more complete context about each member’s needs and experience. That can include information about benefits and coverage, providers, appointments and prior interactions, helping care teams better support members around care plans established by their treating providers.

Previously, Cigna Healthcare case managers had to navigate more than 10 separate clinical and administrative systems to gather this context. Computer use can now help navigate these systems and bring relevant information together in seconds, reducing the time spent searching for information – ultimately giving case managers more time to support members.

“Moving from concept to deployment in under eight weeks shows what’s possible when we bring together AI, our expertise in care management, and the right guardrails for responsible use. More importantly, it means getting better, more complete insights to our case managers sooner, so they can focus their time on what matters most: supporting patients with personalized, compassionate care.”

—Madhu Nutakki, CIO, Cigna Healthcare

Computer use lets agents complete tasks in EHRs and payer portals that APIs don’t reach. In healthcare, that capability is only usable if every action is controlled and auditable. Ambience built additional controls to support that oversight.

In this demonstration, Ambience uses evidence from the patient’s chart to prepare a prior-authorization request on an insurer’s website. When the record is ambiguous, the agent stops and asks the clinician, then waits for approval before submitting. Health systems set which actions the agent can take, can pause it at any point, and get a step-by-step log for audit.

Healthcare startups are helping turn advances in computer use into new ways to support care teams. These five companies are combining AI agents with healthcare expertise to help teams navigate systems, coordinate next steps, and move care forward.

Computer-use agents in healthcare require evaluating clinical safety, protecting patient information, and setting clear limits on what agents can do without human review.

ChatGPT for Healthcare provides role-based access controls and audit logs to support oversight. Organizations can build additional review and approval steps into their workflows and configure the applications and environments agents use to limit access to the records and actions needed for each task. Organization data is not used to train OpenAI foundation models.

To support HIPAA-compliant workflows involving protected health information, organizations must use eligible services covered by their Business Associate Agreement with OpenAI and the required security and retention settings.

Computer-use agents for healthcare are available today in ChatGPT for Healthcare, ChatGPT for Clinicians, and the OpenAI API. Here’s how healthcare organizations, clinicians, and developers can get started.

• Healthcare organizations: Contact our sales team⁠ to discuss using AI in your clinical and administrative workflows. Existing customers can ask their workspace administrator to enable computer use in ChatGPT Work and Codex.

• Individual clinicians: U.S. clinicians can sign up for a free ChatGPT for Clinicians account today⁠(opens in a new window) and experience computer use in ChatGPT Work and Codex.

• Developers: Build healthcare applications with the OpenAI API⁠(opens in a new window), and explore our computer use guide⁠(opens in a new window) to build agents that work across existing software.

We hope these advances enable healthcare teams to spend less time moving information through systems and more time caring for patients.
